ぜんぶ たべちゃった! — He ate it all!
You say that you finished something completely (ぜんぶ たべて しまった) or that something happened that you regret or didn’t mean to do (なくして しまった), and you use the casual form ～ちゃう / ～じゃう.
to finish completely; to do something (by mistake, with regret)
to tidy up, to put away
to be found, to turn up
without meaning to, out of habit
Oh, I drank it (without meaning to).
To say that you finished something completely, all the way: the form ～て + しまう (ぜんぶ たべて しまった).
To express regret or a mistake: なくして しまった, わすれて しまった (“unfortunately”, “without meaning to”).
To use the casual form ～ちゃう / ～じゃう (たべちゃった, のんじゃった).
To use うっかり and つい for “carelessly” and “without meaning to”.
To review ～そう, ～みたい, ～たら and あげる / くれる / もらう from earlier chapters.
May 18, nine in the morning. Kenji’s restaurant is closed today. Mihai, Ana, Kenji, Haruka and Sakura are cleaning up after the party.
Kenji, where’s the rest of the cake? We put it in the fridge yesterday, didn’t we?
Oh… sorry. I got hungry this morning and ate the whole thing.
The whole thing? There was about half left!
It was so good, and I just couldn’t stop… Now I’m so full I can’t move.
Then, Kenji, you sit down. I’ll wash all the plates, every last one.
Oh no! The memory card isn’t in my camera! I lost it!
Calm down, Sakura. Where did you last see it?
This morning, at the hotel, I took the card out of the camera… and then maybe I put it in my pocket.
I hung that jacket on the chair this morning, after we got here.
(Searching the pocket) Here it is! Phew… I thought all the photos were gone.
So this afternoon you two are going back to Hiroshima. I’m going to miss you.
And we leave on our honeymoon tomorrow. The restaurant will get really quiet.
Dad, as punishment for eating the whole cake, you carry our bags to the airport!
belly (“onaka ga suku” = to be hungry)
full (“onaka ga ippai” = full after eating)
I put it in (= irete shimatta)
you ate it all (= tabete shimatta)
cha-t-ta: a tiny pause (っ) before “ta”. たべちゃった = ta-be-cha-t-ta. Without the pause it sounds wrong.
shi-ma-i-ma-shi-ta: the “i” in the last “shi” is barely heard: “shimaimashta”.
kuu-koo: two long vowels. If you shorten them (“koko”), it means “here”!
しまう originally means “to put away, to store”. Attached to the ～て form of another verb, it means the action was done COMPLETELY, it is “closed”. It conjugates like any -u verb:
I’ll eat it all / I’ll end up eating it
I ate it all / I ate it (unfortunately)
You already know the ～て form: たべる → たべて, のむ → のんで, いく → いって, する → して. If ～て ends in で, it stays で: のんで しまう.
Don’t confuse it with the exclamation しまった! (ch. 15) = “Oh no! / Oops, I messed up!”. It’s exactly the same verb, in the past, said on its own.
It shows the action is fully finished, with nothing left to do. In English we say “finish off”, “all of it”, “get it done”:
Kenji ate the whole cake (there’s nothing left).
I read this whole book in one night.
I’ll finish my homework first (to get it out of the way).
I’ll wash all the plates, you sit down.
In the present, ～て しまう sounds like “I’ll finish it and be done with it”. It’s very natural with ぜんぶ, もう, さき に.
3. Meaning 2: regret, a mistake, “without meaning to”
Most often, ～て しまった shows that something happened that you did NOT want or that you regret. In English: “unfortunately”, “I accidentally…”, “I went and…”, “without meaning to”:
I lost the memory card! (what a shame!)
I left my wallet at home.
I watched the film and burst into tears (couldn’t help it).
The train left (and I missed it).
Two adverbs that go hand in hand with this meaning: うっかり = carelessly, absent-mindedly (うっかり わすれて しまった); つい = without meaning to, out of habit, I couldn’t resist (つい たべて しまった).
The same sentence can have both meanings! ケーキ を ぜんぶ たべて しまった = “I ate the whole cake” (done) and, at the same time, “too bad I ate it”. Context and tone decide.
4. The casual form: ～ちゃう / ～じゃう
Among friends and family, ～て しまう “melts” into ～ちゃう, and ～で しまう into ～じゃう. They still conjugate like -u verbs (ちゃった, ちゃいます):
The rule is simple: ～て しま → ～ちゃ, ～で しま → ～じゃ. The rest (う, った, います) stays the same.
The forms ～ちゃう / ～じゃう are conversational. At work, in a letter or in an exam, write ～て しまいました.
5. Combining it with what you already know
～て しまう combines easily with structures from earlier chapters:
It seems he answered in Japanese (by mistake). (～よう, ch. 25)
If you don’t hurry, the plane will leave! (～と, ch. 24)
If you forget, send me a message. (～たら, ch. 22)
Sakura looked like she was about to cry. (～そう, ch. 25)

アナ の メモ — Ana’s list
Ana stuck a list on the fridge door at the restaurant. In the evening, next to each line, she wrote what had happened.
1. Wash the plates. → Mihai washed all of them. Not a single one left.
2. Give the rest of the cake to Mrs Suzuki. → Kenji ate it. Too bad!
3. Put away the lanterns. → I dropped one and it broke.
4. Sakura’s photos. → The memory card turned up, safe and sound!
5. Packing for the honeymoon. → Not yet. I’ll do it all tonight.

さくら の さいご の いちにち — Sakura’s last day
On the morning of the day she was finally going back to Hiroshima, Sakura woke up early.
She could only stay in Madrid for half a day more. It seemed a waste to spend it sleeping.
Her mother was still asleep. Sakura took her camera and quietly opened the hotel window.
Madrid in the morning was blue and shining. Sakura took a photo of the sky.
Down in the street, the baker had already opened his shop. The smell of warm bread rose all the way up to the window.
Then the two of them went to Kenji’s restaurant. Inside, after the party, it was a mess.
Glasses, plates, lanterns and a hat that someone had forgotten.
Ana and Mihai had already started cleaning. Sakura helped too.
She wiped the tables, lined up the chairs and picked up the paper from the floor.
But the rest of the cake was nowhere to be found. Dad had eaten the whole thing that morning.
Mom, exasperated, said: “You’re always like this.” Dad still had a bit of cream on his chin.
Laughing, Sakura pointed the camera at him.
Dad said: “Don’t take a picture!”, but Sakura answered: “Oh yes, I definitely will.”
But when she pressed the shutter button, nothing happened. Sakura looked at the camera and froze. The memory card was gone.
All the wedding photos were on that card. More than two hundred.
“What do I do… I lost it…” Tears welled up in Sakura’s eyes.
Everyone searched. Under the tables, in the garbage bags, under the trees in the garden.
In the end, her mother checked the pocket of the jacket hanging on the chair. The little card was right there.
“You put it in there by accident this morning, didn’t you?” said her mother. Sakura held the card to her chest and wouldn’t let go of it.
In the afternoon they all went to the airport. As punishment, Dad carried all the bags.
The airport was crowded and noisy. Sakura held Ana’s hand tightly the whole time.
When check-in was over, it was already time to say goodbye.
First, her mother handed Ana a small bag. “These are momiji manjū from Hiroshima. Eat them together on your trip.”
Dad looked at the bag and said: “Put it in your bag quickly. I might eat them all.” Everyone laughed.
Sakura took a small envelope out of her bag. “Ana, this is for you. I wanted to give it to you.”
Inside there was a photo. Apparently she had asked someone at the hotel early that morning to print it for her.
It was the photo of the hora. Everyone dancing in a big circle: Spanish people, Romanians, Japanese people, and Tama.
In the middle of the circle, Ana and Sakura were holding hands and laughing with their mouths wide open.
“I lent my camera to Yuki and she took it for us.”
On the back, again in hiragana, it said: “Thank you for becoming my big sister.”
Ana couldn’t say a word. She hugged Sakura tight.
Mihai looked up and blinked again and again. “I got something in my eye,” he said, but nobody believed him.
Mom said to Dad: “Eat properly, okay? Not just cake.”
Dad laughed and promised: “I’ll come home to Hiroshima for the summer holidays.”
At the boarding gate, Sakura kept turning around and waving.
“You absolutely have to send me photos from your honeymoon!”
And then their figures disappeared into the crowd.
The car was quiet on the way back. Dad said softly: “They’re gone.”
Ana looked at the photo on her lap and answered: “But we’ll see each other again. For sure.”
At a red light, Mihai quietly checked the tickets in his pocket. Losing them would be a disaster.
Through the window they could see a plane slowly climbing into the sky.
That evening, Ana packed her suitcase. She put the photo of the hora in last, on top of everything.
Tomorrow it was their turn to leave: for the village in the Carpathians where Mihai’s grandfather was waiting for them.
